title: Planets
notes: Cited for: inner rocky planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars); gas giants Jupiter and Saturn; ice giants Uranus and Neptune.

title: Jupiter: Facts
notes: Cited for: Jupiter is the largest planet and more than twice as massive as all other planets combined.

title: Saturn: Facts
notes: Cited for: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of ice with some rock.

title: What Causes the Seasons?
notes: Cited for: seasons are caused by Earth's ~23.5° axial tilt, not distance from the Sun; hemispheres have opposite seasons.

title: Earth: Facts
notes: Cited for: Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January. Confirm exact page wording.

title: Moon: Facts
notes: Cited for: average Earth–Moon distance ~384,400 km; the Moon is tidally locked, always showing the same face.

title: Moon Phases
notes: Cited for: phases come from how much of the sunlit half we see; a full cycle takes about 29.5 days.

title: Eclipses
notes: Cited for: solar eclipse (Moon between Sun and Earth); lunar eclipse (Earth's shadow falls on the Moon); Sun ~400× wider and ~400× farther than the Moon.

title: What Is a Light-Year?
notes: Cited for: a light-year is a distance (~9.46 trillion km); Proxima Centauri is ~4.2 light-years away.

title: Stars
notes: Cited for: stars form in clouds of gas and dust; hotter stars are bluer; the Sun will become a red giant then a white dwarf; massive stars can end in supernovae.

title: Galaxies
notes: Cited for: Milky Way ~100,000 light-years across; Andromeda ~2.5 million light-years away; the observable universe holds billions of galaxies.

title: How Old Is the Universe?
notes: Cited for: the universe is about 13.8 billion years old.

title: How many oceans are there?
notes: Cited for: one global ocean; 71 percent of Earth covered by water; four historic oceans plus the Southern Ocean as the fifth.

title: How Much Water is There on Earth?
notes: Cited for: about 71 percent of Earth's surface is water-covered.

title: Continent
notes: Cited for: seven continents and their order by size; Asia holds almost a third of the land; Antarctica has no permanent population; Australia smallest and flattest.

title: There's a new ocean now: can you name all five?
notes: Cited for: National Geographic began recognizing the Southern Ocean, encircling Antarctica, as the fifth ocean on World Oceans Day (June 8) 2021.

title: What is the largest ocean on Earth?
notes: Cited for: Pacific is the largest and deepest basin; all continents could fit in it; ranking Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic.

title: Pacific Ocean
notes: Cited for: the Pacific occupies about one-third of the globe's surface and exceeds the whole land surface.

title: Selecting a Map Projection
notes: Cited for: every flat map has distortion; Mercator 1569; Africa is fourteen times larger than Greenland; equal-area maps keep true relative sizes but distort shape.

title: Mercator projection
notes: Cited for: introduced by Gerardus Mercator in 1569; straight lines are lines of constant bearing for navigation; areas far from the Equator appear too large.

title: What is latitude?
notes: Cited for: latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, 0 to 90 degrees; latitude lines are parallel; Equator divides the hemispheres.

title: What is longitude?
notes: Cited for: longitude measures distance east or west of the prime meridian through Greenwich; meridians run pole to pole and meet at the poles.

title: International Prime Meridian Conference
notes: Cited for: the 1884 Washington conference chose the Greenwich meridian as 0 degrees longitude; countries had used their own prime meridians; standard time zones adopted.

title: What is at Zero Degrees Latitude and Zero Degrees Longitude?
notes: Cited for: 0 degrees latitude, 0 degrees longitude is in the Atlantic Ocean in the Gulf of Guinea; Null Island nickname; faulty records assigned 0,0.

title: Equator
notes: Cited for: Equator at 0 degrees latitude, halfway between the poles; divides the hemispheres; Sun directly over it at the equinoxes.

title: Tropics
notes: Cited for: Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn at 23.5 degrees north and south of the Equator.

title: Tropic of Cancer
notes: Cited for: about 23 degrees 27 minutes N; the Sun is directly over it at the June solstice, its northernmost overhead position.

title: Tropic of Capricorn
notes: Cited for: about 23 degrees 27 minutes S; the Sun is directly over it around December 21, its southernmost overhead position.

title: Lahaina Noon
notes: Cited for: when the Sun is exactly overhead an upright object casts no shadow; the Sun is never directly overhead outside the tropics; Hawaii is the only US state where it happens.

title: Arctic Circle
notes: Cited for: about 66 degrees 30 minutes N; the Sun does not set about June 21 or rise about December 21; continuous day or night grows to six months at the pole; tilt of about 23.5 degrees.

title: Antarctic Circle
notes: Cited for: Antarctic Circle at 66 degrees 30 minutes S, with at least one day of continuous daylight and of darkness a year.

title: Standard Time
notes: Cited for: communities once kept separate local times; railways made standard time urgent; 24 zones on meridians 15 degrees apart from Greenwich; borders follow political boundaries.

title: International Date Line
notes: Cited for: date line follows the 180th meridian for most of its length; travelers going west set calendars a day ahead, east a day back.

title: Date Line
notes: Cited for: date line roughly follows the 180-degree meridian halfway around from the prime meridian; west is one day ahead; it curves around Kiribati.

title: The Sun, Earth and Cardinal Directions
notes: Cited for: the four cardinal directions; the Sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west; east and west at right angles to north and south.

title: Why does the Sun rise in the east?
notes: Cited for: Earth rotates toward the east, so the Sun rises in the east and moves westward across the sky.

title: Earth's Magnetic Field (compass needles)
notes: Cited for: Earth is like a giant magnet; compass needles follow magnetic field lines; Magnetic North Pole differs from the Geographic North Pole and moves; magnetic declination.

title: Compass (navigational instrument)
notes: Cited for: a magnetized needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field; needles point to a point near, not at, the North Pole; variation or declination varies from place to place.

title: Wandering of the Geomagnetic Poles
publisher: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
notes: Cited for: the magnetic dip poles migrate over time.

title: Topographic Maps
notes: Cited for: contour lines connect points of the same elevation above a reference surface, usually mean sea level; spacing shows steepness.

title: Topographic Maps
notes: Cited for: contour lines are lines of equal elevation; the closer the contours, the steeper the slope.

title: Mount Everest
notes: Cited for: Everest is the highest mountain in the world at about 8,849 m; 2020 China and Nepal joint measurement.

title: Plateau
notes: Cited for: a plateau is a flat, elevated landform that rises sharply above the surrounding area on at least one side.

title: Valleys, Information and Facts
notes: Cited for: valleys are low areas carved by water and ice; rivers carve V shapes and glaciers grind them into U shapes.

title: Delta
notes: Cited for: a delta is a flat, low-lying plain at a river's mouth built from sediment dropped as the river slows; named for the Greek letter delta.

title: Space Segment
notes: Cited for: at least 24 operational GPS satellites; each circles Earth twice a day at about 20,200 km; users can view at least four satellites from virtually anywhere.

title: GPS: The Global Positioning System
notes: Cited for: satellites transmit one-way signals with position and time; receivers calculate three-dimensional position and time; civilian service freely available to all users.

title: Global Positioning System
notes: Cited for: each satellite transmits its position and time; a receiver finds its position from how long the signals took to reach it.

title: The Global Positioning System (Geodesy tutorial)
notes: Cited for: satellites carry very precise clocks; distance equals signal speed times travel time; four satellites needed, three for position and one for the receiver's clock error.

title: What Is An Antipode In Geography?
notes: Cited for: antipode definition; noon at one is midnight at the other; opposite hemispheres; about 15% of land is antipodal to land; Spain's antipodes in New Zealand.

title: Antipodes World Map & Why You Can't Dig To China From The US
notes: Cited for: digging through Earth from the US leads to the Indian Ocean, not China; about 15% of land is antipodal to land.

title: Crust
notes: Cited for: oceanic crust is 5 to 10 km thick; continental crust can reach 70 km.

title: Mantle
notes: Cited for: the mantle is about 2,900 km thick and makes up 84 percent of Earth's volume.

title: Core
notes: Cited for: core begins about 2,900 km down; iron and nickel; liquid outer core makes the magnetic field; solid inner core as hot as the Sun's surface; S-wave shadow.

title: How Deep Is the Deepest Hole in the World?
notes: Cited for: the Kola Superdeep Borehole reached 12,262 m after about 20 years of drilling.

title: Earth Fact Sheet
notes: Cited for: Earth's volumetric mean radius is 6,371 km.

title: Are the tectonic plates floating on magma?
notes: Cited for: mantle rock is solid but flows slowly, about as fast as fingernails grow; the outer core is the only entirely liquid layer.

title: Inside the Earth (This Dynamic Earth)
notes: Cited for: the lithosphere is broken into moving plates that carry continents and oceans; plates move on the slowly flowing asthenosphere.

title: Understanding plate motions (This Dynamic Earth)
notes: Cited for: divergent, convergent and transform boundaries; Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads about 2.5 cm a year; Atlantic grew from a tiny inlet; Iceland is splitting.

title: Plate Tectonics
notes: Cited for: the lithosphere is broken into plates moved by convection; plates move 2 to 15 cm a year.

title: Will California eventually fall into the ocean?
notes: Cited for: the Pacific Plate moves northwest past the North American Plate about 46 mm a year; Los Angeles and San Francisco will one day be adjacent.

title: Historical perspective (This Dynamic Earth)
notes: Cited for: Wegener's 1912 continental drift; Pangaea breaking up about 200 million years ago; coastline fit and fossil evidence; no mechanism.

title: Pangea
notes: Cited for: Pangea proposed by Wegener in 1912; name from Greek for 'all the Earth'; surrounded by Panthalassa; began breaking apart about 200 million years ago.

title: Continental Drift
notes: Cited for: coastlines and rock layers of South America and Africa fit; Mesosaurus fossils; drift rejected for lack of a mechanism until the 1960s.

title: The Science of Earthquakes
notes: Cited for: earthquakes are sudden slips on faults after stuck plate edges; hypocenter and epicenter; seismic waves like ripples; seismographs.

title: Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity
notes: Cited for: each whole-number magnitude step is ten times the amplitude and about 32 times the energy.

title: Valdivia Earthquake Strikes Chile
notes: Cited for: May 22, 1960 magnitude 9.5 Chile earthquake, the most powerful recorded; its tsunami crossed the Pacific and killed 61 in Hilo.

title: Tsunami Historical Series: Chile - 1960
notes: Cited for: largest earthquake recorded by instruments, magnitude 9.5; tsunami took almost 15 hours to reach Hawaii and killed 61 in Hilo.

title: How do volcanoes erupt?
notes: Cited for: magma is lighter than surrounding rock so it rises; erupted magma is called lava.

title: Ring of Fire
notes: Cited for: about 40,000 km long; 75 percent of volcanoes (more than 450) and 90 percent of earthquakes; subducted rock melts into magma.

title: Hotspots: Mantle thermal plumes (This Dynamic Earth)
notes: Cited for: most eruptions occur near plate boundaries; Hawaii is over 3,200 km from a boundary, above a stationary hotspot; islands get older away from it.

title: What is a tsunami?
notes: Cited for: tsunamis caused by undersea earthquakes or eruptions; as fast as jet planes over deep water; slow and grow in shallow water; 'tidal wave' discouraged.

title: Life of a Tsunami
notes: Cited for: seafloor uplift pushes the whole water column; open-ocean waves at most several meters high; amplitude grows near shore; sea recedes first.

title: The Tsunami Story
notes: Cited for: tsunami is Japanese for 'harbor wave'; tsunamis frequently occur in the Pacific where dense ocean plates slide under lighter continental plates.

title: The Himalayas: Two continents collide (This Dynamic Earth)
notes: Cited for: India 6,400 km south of Asia 80 million years ago moving about 9 m a century; collision 40 to 50 million years ago; similar density; rising more than 1 cm a year.

title: The Ordovician rocks of Mount Everest
notes: Cited for: the summit rocks of Everest are limestones deposited in a shallow sea, containing fossils of marine animals.

title: How Did Marine Fossils End Up on Top of Mount Everest?
notes: Cited for: the limestone atop Everest was once ocean floor and holds many marine fossils.

title: The Rock Cycle
notes: Cited for: three main rock types and how each forms; slow cooling makes large crystals; any rock type can become any other.

title: Magma's Role in the Rock Cycle
notes: Cited for: magma that cools into a solid is igneous rock; erupted magma is called lava; basalt forms from cooled lava.

title: Metamorphic Rocks
notes: Cited for: limestone changes into marble and granite into gneiss under heat and pressure.

title: What are metamorphic rocks?
notes: Cited for: metamorphism changes rock without melting it.

title: Limestone
notes: Cited for: limestone is a sedimentary rock whose grains are often fragments of fossil shells from lime-secreting sea life.

title: Erosion
notes: Cited for: weathering versus erosion; water as the major agent, plus wind and ice; caves, arches and sea stacks; wind shaping rock and dunes.

title: Geology (Grand Canyon National Park)
notes: Cited for: the Colorado River began carving the canyon 5 to 6 million years ago; flood-borne rocks act like chisels.

title: Grand Canyon Fly-through Animation
notes: Cited for: the canyon is one mile (1.6 km) deep and was carved by the Colorado River.

title: Tectonic Movements
notes: Cited for: at Þingvellir the plates break apart and the land between subsides in a 7 km wide rift; about 2 cm a year.

title: Inside Out: Why Iceland is a Rare Window into the Earth?
notes: Cited for: Iceland's west and east are on the North American and Eurasian plates pulling apart; the ridge is almost all hidden; hot spot volcanism.

title: Water Cycle

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.5 The Small and Large Intestines
notes: Cited for: most digestion and practically all absorption happen in the small intestine; villi and microvilli enlarge its absorptive surface.

title: Surface area of the digestive tract, revisited (Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology, 2014)
notes: Cited for: Helander and Fandriks measured the inner surface of the adult digestive tract at about 30 to 40 square meters, mostly small intestine, about 2 square meters large intestine.

title: The surface area of the digestive tract 'only' as large as a studio apartment
notes: Cited for: earlier reference works gave 180 to 300 square meters, a tennis court or more; the 2014 measurement is about half a badminton court.

title: Liver
notes: Cited for: the liver is the largest gland, 1.2 to 1.6 kg in adults; makes bile; stores glycogen and vitamins; destroys old red blood cells; removes wastes; portal vein brings nutrient-rich blood from the digestive system.

title: Hepatectomy (Liver Resection)
notes: Cited for: up to two-thirds of a healthy liver can be removed; healthy liver tissue regenerates in weeks, sometimes months.

title: Cellular and Molecular Basis of Liver Regeneration (Seminars in Cell and Developmental Biology, 2020)
publisher: Seminars in Cell and Developmental Biology (via PubMed Central)
notes: Cited for: after removal of two-thirds of the liver it grows back to essentially its original size; the Prometheus myth.

title: Prometheus
notes: Cited for: Zeus sent an eagle to eat Prometheus's liver, which constantly replenished itself.

title: Your Kidneys & How They Work
publisher: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK)
notes: Cited for: two bean-shaped, fist-sized kidneys below the rib cage; about a million nephrons each; glomerulus filters, tubule returns needed substances; about 150 quarts filtered to 1 to 2 quarts of urine.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 25.5 Physiology of Urine Formation
notes: Cited for: about 150 to 180 liters of filtrate a day; 99 percent returned by reabsorption; about 1 to 2 liters of urine a day.

title: Carbohydrates
notes: Cited for: carbohydrates, proteins and fats are the three main nutrients; carbohydrates (sugars, starches, fiber) become glucose, the main energy source; the body cannot break down most fiber.

title: Dietary Fats
notes: Cited for: fats give energy, twice the calories of proteins or carbohydrates, and help the body absorb vitamins.

title: Protein in diet
notes: Cited for: proteins are chains of amino acids; essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and come from food; nonessential ones the body makes.

title: Vitamins
notes: Cited for: vitamins are needed for normal cell function, growth and development; there are 13 essential vitamins.

title: Minerals
notes: Cited for: the body uses minerals to keep bones, muscles, heart and brain working; calcium and phosphorus are macrominerals.

title: Micronutrients
notes: Cited for: micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed by the body in very small amounts, yet critical for health.

title: Calorie
notes: Cited for: a calorie is the heat that raises 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius; the food Calorie is a kilocalorie of 1,000 calories.

title: Calories (MSD Manual Consumer Version)
notes: Cited for: a calorie is a measure of energy; food energy is released in digestion and used by cells; needs vary with age, sex, weight, activity and metabolic rate.

title: Atwater-Rosa calorimeter
notes: Cited for: developed by Atwater and Rosa, 1892 to 1897; proved the conservation of energy in human beings; made it possible to calculate the energy values of foods.

title: Counting Calories
notes: Cited for: Atwater's respiration calorimeter chamber and its more than 500 measurements of human heat and carbon dioxide output.

title: Going Nuts Over Calories
notes: Cited for: the Atwater system, about 4 calories per gram of protein and carbohydrate and 9 per gram of fat, is used to calculate the calorie content of foods.

title: Appraising the brain's energy budget (PNAS, 2002)
publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
notes: Cited for: the brain is about 2 percent of body weight but accounts for about 20 percent of the oxygen and calories the body uses, at a remarkably constant rate.

title: Vitamin C
notes: Cited for: needed to make collagen; humans and some other animals cannot make it; scurvy symptoms; destroyed by heat; isolated 1928 and identified as the antiscorbutic factor in 1932.

title: Vitamin C: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
notes: Cited for: scurvy signs can appear within about a month of very low intake; impaired collagen synthesis weakens connective tissue; bleeding gums, loose teeth, poor wound healing; fatal untreated.

title: Vitamin C (Advances in Nutrition, 2023)
notes: Cited for: primates, guinea pigs, bats and some fish and birds lost the ability to make vitamin C; its role in making collagen; scurvy signs.

title: James Lind and scurvy: 1747 to 1795
notes: Cited for: the prospective controlled trial of six treatments in 12 patients on HMS Salisbury from 20 May 1747; one citrus patient fit for duty after six days; Lind's rob; heat destroys ascorbic acid; Admiralty adoption in 1795 after Blane.

title: The mysteries of James Lind and scurvy
notes: Cited for: the six remedies given to six pairs; the citrus pair's results; Lind's theory of moisture and poorly digested diet; lemon juice ordered for sailors in 1795.

title: James Lind's Treatise of the Scurvy (1753) (Postgraduate Medical Journal, 2002)
notes: Cited for: Lind saw scurvy as a disease of faulty digestion, not dietary deficiency, and did not clearly declare citrus the definitive cure.

title: James Lind
notes: Cited for: Lind's comparison of citrus with other remedies as an early example of a clinical trial; adopted by the Royal Navy in 1795.

title: Metabolic Disorders
notes: Cited for: metabolism is how the body gets or makes energy from food; fuel is used right away or stored in the liver, muscles and body fat.

title: Cellular respiration
notes: Cited for: cells combine oxygen with food molecules to release their chemical energy; in eukaryotic cells the steps are located in mitochondria.

title: Brain Basics: Know Your Brain
publisher: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH)
notes: Cited for: cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem jobs; the four lobes; hemispheres, corpus callosum and crossover control; language mainly left; hippocampus as memory indexer; hypothalamus and adrenaline; neuron parts, myelin and synapses.

title: Brain Basics: The Life and Death of a Neuron
publisher: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH)
notes: Cited for: neurons use electrical and chemical signals; cell body, axon and dendrites; neurotransmitters cross the synapse; sensory neurons carry information to the brain and motor neurons carry messages to the muscles.

title: Brain Basics: Understanding Sleep
publisher: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH)
notes: Cited for: a third of life asleep; non-REM stages 1 to 3 and REM; REM about 90 minutes in; limb paralysis in REM; cycles and longer REM later; purpose a mystery; memory consolidation; dreaming about two hours a night, most vivid in REM.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 12.1 Basic Structure and Function of the Nervous System
notes: Cited for: CNS is brain and spinal cord, PNS everything else; skull and vertebral column; sensation, integration and response (batter example); voluntary (somatic) and involuntary (autonomic) responses.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 12.2 Nervous Tissue
notes: Cited for: information flows one way through a neuron, from dendrites across the cell body and down the axon; myelin insulates axons.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e, Chapter 14 Introduction (The Somatic Nervous System)
notes: Cited for: the hot-stove withdrawal reflex path from skin sensors through the spinal cord to a motor neuron and the biceps.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 14.3 Motor Responses
notes: Cited for: simple somatic reflexes do not include higher centers; inhibiting the triceps makes withdrawal faster; stretch reflex and the knee jerk.

title: Anatomy & Physiology 2e, 13.4 Ventral Horn Output and Reflexes
notes: Cited for: withdrawal typically before the pain is registered; stretch reflex is monosynaptic and very fast; head jerking back up when nodding off.

title: Equal numbers of neuronal and nonneuronal cells make the human brain an isometrically scaled-up primate brain (Journal of Comparative Neurology, 2009)
notes: Cited for: Azevedo et al. counted on average about 86 billion neurons and about 85 billion nonneuronal cells in adult male brains using the isotropic fractionator.

title: Are There Really as Many Neurons in the Human Brain as Stars in the Milky Way?
notes: Cited for: the old 100 billion figure had no peer-reviewed count behind it; the 2009 method dissolved cell membranes into an even soup and counted stained nuclei.

title: The human brain in numbers: a linearly scaled-up primate brain (Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 2009)
notes: Cited for: cerebral cortex about 82 percent of brain mass with about 16 billion neurons (19 percent); cerebellum about 10 percent of mass with about 69 billion neurons.

title: An Evaluation of the Left-Brain vs. Right-Brain Hypothesis with Resting State Functional Connectivity Magnetic Resonance Imaging (PLOS ONE, 2013)
notes: Cited for: Nielsen et al. analyzed resting scans of 1,011 people aged 7 to 29; lateralization is local; no whole-brain left-brained or right-brained phenotype; language hubs lateralized left.

title: Researchers Debunk Myth of "Right-brain" and "Left-brain" Personality Traits
notes: Cited for: the popular logical-left and creative-right idea; 1,011 people, about 7,000 regions; no evidence people use one side more; language tends left and attention right.

title: Cerebral hemisphere
notes: Cited for: each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body; the corpus callosum links them; speech area in the left hemisphere for most people; right hemisphere leads in spatial tasks.

title: The Curious Case of Patient H.M.
notes: Cited for: Henry Molaison, 27, had tissue removed from each side of his brain in 1953 to control seizures; could not form new memories; improved at mirror tracing without recalling it.

title: Hermann Ebbinghaus
notes: Cited for: Ebbinghaus tested himself with nonsense syllables; Uber das Gedachtnis (1885); the forgetting curve relating forgetting to time.

title: Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve (PLOS ONE, 2015)
notes: Cited for: Ebbinghaus used only himself as subject; forgetting is steep soon after learning and slows over time.

title: Distributing Learning Over Time: The Spacing Effect in Children's Acquisition and Generalization of Science Concepts (Child Development, 2012)
notes: Cited for: long-term memory is better when learning is spaced out rather than massed; Ebbinghaus ran the first study; one of the most replicated findings in psychology.

title: Brain may flush out toxins during sleep
notes: Cited for: a 2013 NIH-funded mouse study (Nedergaard, published in Science) suggested space between brain cells grows during sleep so fluid can flush out toxins.

title: Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia (Nature Neuroscience, 2024)
notes: Cited for: Miao, Franks, Wisden and colleagues found that brain clearance was reduced, not increased, in sleeping mice.

title: Who discovered REM sleep? (SLEEP, 2024)
notes: Cited for: Aserinsky and Kleitman, University of Chicago, published the 1953 Science paper on periods of rapid eye movements in sleep and woke sleepers to find they were dreaming.

title: The Stubborn Scientist Who Unraveled a Mystery of the Night
notes: Cited for: in December 1951 Eugene Aserinsky tested his recording machine on his 8-year-old son Armond; rapid eye movements correlated with recall of vivid dreams.

title: The Interpretation of Dreams
notes: Cited for: Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams (1899) argued dreams are disguised wish fulfillments.

title: The brain as a dream state generator: an activation-synthesis hypothesis of the dream process (American Journal of Psychiatry, 1977)
notes: Cited for: Hobson and McCarley proposed that dreams are the forebrain making sense of signals generated by the brainstem during REM sleep.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 17.1 An Overview of the Endocrine System
notes: Cited for: neurotransmitters act locally within milliseconds; hormones travel in the bloodstream and act more slowly; fight-or-flight hormones within seconds because nerves trigger the adrenal glands.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 17.6 The Adrenal Glands
notes: Cited for: adrenal medulla releases epinephrine (adrenaline) under a nerve pathway from the hypothalamus; raised heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose; wider airways; blood diverted from gut and skin; dry mouth, lost appetite, wide pupils.

title: Fight-or-flight response
notes: Cited for: Walter Cannon described the response in the early 1900s and coined the phrase; sympathetic nerves trigger hormone release.

title: Does Thinking Really Hard Burn More Calories?
notes: Cited for: brain about 2 percent of body weight, 20 percent of resting metabolic rate; hard mental tasks add only a tiny amount.

title: Human sensory reception
notes: Cited for: Aristotle described at least five senses; the modern catalog adds receptors in muscles, tendons and joints (kinesthetic sense), vestibular organs (balance), heat and pain receptors, and digestive-tract receptors behind hunger and thirst.

title: Proprioceptor
notes: Cited for: proprioceptors in muscles, tendons, joints and skin keep a continuous report on limb position and movement.

title: Human senses and sensors from Aristotle to the present (Frontiers in Neurology, 2024)
notes: Cited for: Aristotle first listed five senses in De Anima; the debate over five, six or seven senses is still alive; the authors propose the vestibular system and proprioception as a sixth and seventh sense; classification features are used inconsistently.

title: Aristotle, De Anima (On the Soul), Book III, translated by J. A. Smith
publisher: Classics in the History of Psychology (York University)
notes: Cited for: Book III opens by arguing there is no sixth sense beyond the five enumerated (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch).

title: Humans could have as many as 33 senses (The Conversation, December 2025)
notes: Cited for: philosopher Barry Smith reports that neuroscientist Charles Spence's colleagues put the number of senses anywhere between 22 and 33; proprioception, balance and interoception as senses beyond the five.

title: Aristotle got it wrong: We have a lot more than five senses
notes: Cited for: Barry C. Smith says there could be anything between 22 and 33 senses and that there is a lot of argument about it.

title: Psychology 2e, 5.1 Sensation versus Perception
notes: Cited for: the five-senses notion is oversimplified (balance, proprioception, pain, temperature); transduction; perception as organizing and interpreting sensation; sensory adaptation.

title: How the Eyes Work
notes: Cited for: cornea bends light; iris controls the pupil; lens and cornea focus light on the retina; photoreceptors turn light into electrical signals that travel through the optic nerve to the brain.

title: Why is the visual image projected on the retina of the human eye upside down?
notes: Cited for: the cornea and lens act together as a convex lens, forming an inverted image on the retina, which the brain corrects so we perceive the world upright.

title: Blind spot
notes: Cited for: the blind spot corresponds to the optic disk, which has no rods or cones; the two eyes' overlapping fields and the brain's filling-in hide it.

title: Color vision deficiency (MedlinePlus Genetics)
publisher: MedlinePlus Genetics (NIH National Library of Medicine)
notes: Cited for: rods for low light, cones for bright light and color; three cone types; red-green defects are the most common form, about 1 in 12 males and 1 in 200 females of Northern European ancestry; OPN1LW and OPN1MW genes on the X chromosome.

title: Color Blindness
notes: Cited for: about 1 in 12 men have color vision deficiency; men have a much higher risk than women. (The current page gives no figure for women; the 1 in 200 figure is cited from MedlinePlus Genetics.)

title: Causes of Color Vision Deficiency
notes: Cited for: genes for red-green color vision deficiency are passed down on the X chromosome; males have one X, females need the gene on both.

title: Types of Color Vision Deficiency
notes: Cited for: the most common type of color vision deficiency makes it hard to tell red from green.

title: John Dalton and colour blindness
publisher: Science and Industry Museum (Science Museum Group)
notes: Cited for: Dalton's 1794 account to the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society; his blue vitreous humour theory; the 1844 post-mortem finding the humours colourless; later DNA analysis showing he lacked the medium-wavelength (green) receptor gene.

title: John Dalton
notes: Cited for: Dalton described the defect in his own and his brother's vision; the first publication on colour blindness, later called Daltonism.

title: Refractive Errors
notes: Cited for: refractive errors happen when the eye's shape keeps light from focusing on the retina; causes include eyeball length, cornea shape and lens aging.

title: Nearsightedness (Myopia)
notes: Cited for: light focuses in front of the retina; far-away objects look blurry; eyeball too long or cornea/lens shape problems.

title: Farsightedness (Hyperopia)
notes: Cited for: light focuses behind the retina; nearby objects look blurry; eyeball too short or cornea/lens shape problems.

title: Concave, convex, and cylinder lenses
notes: Cited for: a concave (minus) lens corrects myopia; a convex (plus) lens corrects hyperopia.

title: Myopia
notes: Cited for: myopia focuses distant images in front of the retina, usually in an eye longer than normal; corrected by concave lenses.

title: Hyperopia
notes: Cited for: hyperopia is corrected by glasses with convex lenses that supply extra convexity for focusing.

title: Contact lens
notes: Cited for: a thin artificial lens worn on the surface of the eye to correct refractive defects, a substitute for eyeglasses.

title: Eyeglasses
notes: Cited for: in Europe eyeglasses first appeared in Italy; the earliest glasses had convex lenses for farsightedness; a concave lens for myopia is first evident in Raphael's portrait of Pope Leo X (1517).

title: How Do We Hear?
publisher: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH)
notes: Cited for: ear canal, eardrum, malleus, incus and stapes, cochlea, basilar membrane, hair cells (high pitches at the wide end, low toward the center), stereocilia, auditory nerve.

title: Noise-Induced Hearing Loss
publisher: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH)
notes: Cited for: most noise-induced hearing loss is caused by damage and death of hair cells; unlike bird and amphibian hair cells, human hair cells don't grow back.

title: Stapes
notes: Cited for: the stapes, or stirrup, is the smallest of the three middle-ear bones and resembles a stirrup.

title: Balance Disorders
publisher: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH)
notes: Cited for: balance relies on eyes, ears, and muscles and touch sensors in the legs; the vestibular system (labyrinth); three fluid-filled semicircular canals at right angles sense rotation; utricle and saccule with calcium carbonate grains sense head position relative to gravity.

title: Spinning and Unspinning
notes: Cited for: after spinning, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving, so the brain gets two different messages and you feel dizzy.

title: Motion Sickness (CDC Yellow Book)
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Cited for: sensory conflict theory; in a ship with limited outside view the vestibular system reports motion while vision suggests none.

title: Taste Disorders
publisher: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH)
notes: Cited for: taste buds on the tongue, roof of the mouth and throat; at least five basic tastes including umami; the separate-regions idea is a misconception; flavor combines tastes, heat, cold, texture and aroma; a blocked nose makes food bland.

title: Smell Disorders
publisher: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH)
notes: Cited for: olfactory sensory neurons high inside the nose; odors reach them through the nostrils and through a channel from the roof of the throat to the nose when chewing.

title: The Taste Map of the Tongue You Learned in School Is All Wrong
notes: Cited for: Hanig's 1901 study found only minute sensitivity differences; Edwin Boring redrew the graph in the 1940s; all areas with taste buds sense all taste qualities.

title: Biology 2e, 36.2 Somatosensation
notes: Cited for: four categories of somatosensory receptors; free nerve endings are the most common in skin and sense pain, hot and cold and light touch; touch receptors denser in fingertips and lips than in hairy skin.

title: Press release: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2021
notes: Cited for: Julius and Patapoutian's prize for receptors for temperature and touch; capsaicin and TRPV1 (painful heat); menthol and TRPM8 (cold); Piezo2 essential for touch and proprioception.

title: Channelopathy-associated congenital insensitivity to pain (MedlinePlus Genetics)
publisher: MedlinePlus Genetics (NIH National Library of Medicine)
notes: Cited for: pain is a vital signal that helps people avoid danger; affected people never feel pain when injured, can tell hot from cold, have more injuries and may have shorter lives; caused by SCN9A variants; rare.

title: Optical illusion
notes: Cited for: an optical illusion is a perception that contradicts objective reality; causes include light, poor lighting, the eye itself and how the brain processes visual information.

title: Muller-Lyer Illusion
notes: Cited for: Franz Carl Muller-Lyer published the illusion in 1889; two identical lines look different lengths because of the fins at their ends.

title: Adelson's Checker-Shadow Illusion
notes: Cited for: Edward Adelson's illusion; tiles A and B are the same shade of grey; the visual system applies lightness constancy, correcting for the depicted shadow.

title: Human skin
notes: Cited for: skin is the body's largest organ, covering its entire surface as a protective barrier.

title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 5.1 Layers of the Skin
notes: Cited for: epidermis, dermis and hypodermis; epidermis is epithelium; stratum corneum of dead keratinized cells blocks microbes and water loss; new cells pushed up from the stratum basale; outer layer replaced in about 4 weeks.

title: The skin microbiome (Nature Reviews Microbiology, 2011)
publisher: Grice and Segre, NHGRI (via PubMed Central)
notes: Cited for: skin is about 1.8 square meters; its surface is cool, acidic and dry; resident microbes protect against invasion by more harmful organisms.

title: Association Between Skin Acid Mantle, Natural Moisturizing Factors, and Antibacterial Activity Against S. aureus in the Stratum Corneum (2023)
notes: Cited for: skin surface pH is on average below 5, and the acidic pH directly inhibits growth of Staphylococcus aureus.

title: Components of skin (health video)
notes: Cited for: sebaceous glands make oil that keeps skin from drying and kills bacteria.

title: Infectious Diseases
notes: Cited for: infectious diseases are caused by germs; the four main kinds are bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites; bacteria are one-celled and can give off toxins.

title: Bacterial Infections
notes: Cited for: bacteria are one-celled living things; most types do not make you sick and some are helpful; antibiotics treat bacterial infections.

title: Viral Infections
notes: Cited for: viruses are genetic material in a protein coat; they invade living cells and use them to multiply; antibiotics do not work for viral infections.

title: Fungal Infections
notes: Cited for: fungi include mushrooms, mold and mildew; they live in air, soil, water and on plants, and some live in the body; athlete's foot is a fungal infection.

title: Virus
notes: Cited for: most viruses are 20 to 400 nanometers across; viruses multiply only in living cells; Ivanovsky (1892) found the tobacco mosaic agent passed through filters that stop bacteria.

title: Immune response
notes: Cited for: innate immunity is the defense you are born with, including skin; phagocytes eat germs; acquired immunity develops with exposure; B and T lymphocytes; antibodies attach to specific antigens; memory speeds later responses.

title: Elie Metchnikoff
notes: Cited for: from 1882 in Messina, cells in starfish larvae engulfed splinters he introduced; he named them phagocytes, "devouring cells"; 1908 Nobel Prize shared with Paul Ehrlich.

title: Fever
notes: Cited for: the hypothalamus regulates body temperature; pyrogens carried in the blood raise its set point; chills as temperature rises, warm flushed moist skin as it falls; higher temperatures stimulate white blood cells and antibodies and may slow some microbes.

title: Fever and the thermal regulation of immunity: the immune system feels the heat (Nature Reviews Immunology, 2015)
publisher: Evans, Repasky and Fisher (via PubMed Central)
notes: Cited for: fever conserved in warm- and cold-blooded vertebrates for over 600 million years; desert iguanas seek heat when infected, and survival falls 75% if prevented from raising temperature about 2 C; each 1 C rise costs 10 to 12.5% more metabolism.

title: Understanding How Vaccines Work
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Cited for: vaccines imitate an infection to engage the body's defenses; a vaccinated person is far less likely to die or become seriously ill.

title: Global immunization efforts have saved at least 154 million lives over the past 50 years
notes: Cited for: a 2024 WHO-led study estimated at least 154 million lives saved since 1974, 6 every minute, 101 million of them infants; immunization is the single greatest contribution of any health intervention to infant survival.

title: Edward Jenner and the history of smallpox and vaccination (Baylor University Medical Center Proceedings, 2005)
notes: Cited for: variolation in Africa, India and China before the 18th century; about 2 to 3% of variolated people died; Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's daughter inoculated in London in 1721; Benjamin Jesty tried cowpox before Jenner.

title: History of Smallpox
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Cited for: variolation scratched material from smallpox sores into the arm or had it inhaled, and fewer died than from natural smallpox; Jenner inoculated James Phipps with cowpox from Sarah Nelmes in 1796.

title: Edward Jenner
notes: Cited for: May 14, 1796 cowpox inoculation of James Phipps; July 1 smallpox challenge, no disease; 1798 Inquiry; vaccination from Latin vacca, cow.

title: Alexander Fleming
notes: Cited for: in September 1928 a Staphylococcus culture was contaminated by Penicillium mold that inhibited the bacteria; Fleming failed to stabilize and purify penicillin; Nobel Prize 1945 shared with Florey and Chain.

title: Alexander Fleming (Scientific Biographies)
notes: Cited for: the culture was left out during a two-week vacation; the spore perhaps came through a window or more likely up a stairwell from the lab below; his 1929 paper drew little notice.

title: Howard Walter Florey and Ernst Boris Chain (Scientific Biographies)
notes: Cited for: 1940 mouse test; February 1941 policeman patient who relapsed when supply ran out despite recovery from urine; mold grown in vessels including hospital bedpans; British-American effort of thousands of people and some 35 institutions.

title: Alexander Fleming (1881-1955): Discoverer of penicillin (Singapore Medical Journal, 2015)
notes: Cited for: Fleming named the mould juice that killed the bacteria penicillin; the 1929 paper met little initial enthusiasm.

title: Ignaz Semmelweis
notes: Cited for: childbed fever deaths two or three times higher in the students' division; a colleague's death from a wound infection; chlorinated lime handwashing; deaths fell from 18.27 to 1.27 percent; authority stood against him.

title: Handwashing Facts
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Cited for: handwashing cuts diarrheal illness 23 to 40% and respiratory illness 16 to 21%; lathering and scrubbing lift microbes from skin; germs reach eyes, nose and mouth from hands.

title: About Handwashing
publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Cited for: soap and water is the best way to get rid of germs in most situations; scrub at least 20 seconds, about two runs of the Happy Birthday song.

title: Allergy
notes: Cited for: an allergy is an immune reaction to something that does not bother most people, a false alarm; common allergens; genes and environment; anaphylaxis can be life-threatening.

title: Allergies
notes: Cited for: if both parents have allergies there is a good chance a child will too; chemicals such as histamine cause symptoms.

title: Allergy
notes: Cited for: IgE antibodies bind mast cells in connective tissue; antigen binding makes mast cells release histamine, which causes a running nose and swelling.

title: IgE and mast cells in allergic disease (Nature Medicine, 2012)
notes: Cited for: IgE binding to mast cells sensitizes them to release mediators such as histamine on later encounters with the same antigen.

title: Diagnosed Allergic Conditions in Adults: United States, 2021 (NCHS Data Brief No. 460)
publisher: CDC National Center for Health Statistics
notes: Cited for: in 2021, 31.8% of US adults had a seasonal allergy, eczema or food allergy.

title: Swollen lymph nodes
notes: Cited for: lymph nodes help the body recognize and fight germs; they are found in the neck, armpit and groin among other places; infections are the most common cause of swelling.

title: Lymphatic Diseases
notes: Cited for: lymph nodes are glands along the lymph vessels; with the spleen, they are where white blood cells fight infection.

title: About Pregnancy
publisher: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development
notes: Cited for: pregnancy usually lasts about 40 weeks, measured from the last menstrual period; conception begins when a sperm penetrates an egg.

title: Fetal development
publisher: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia (US National Library of Medicine)
notes: Cited for: sperm and egg meet and conception occurs; the zygote divides into a ball of cells; gestational age counted from the last menstrual period; embryo called a fetus from the end of week 10 of pregnancy.

title: Meiosis (Talking Glossary of Genomic and Genetic Terms)
notes: Cited for: each egg or sperm has exactly 23 chromosomes, and a fertilized egg has 46.

title: Stem Cell Basics
notes: Cited for: cells of the early embryo develop into the specialized cell types, tissues and organs of the whole body, becoming more specialized step by step.

title: Stem Cell (Talking Glossary of Genomic and Genetic Terms)
notes: Cited for: embryonic stem cells can give rise to neural, muscle and liver cells.

title: Allele (Talking Glossary of Genomic and Genetic Terms)
notes: Cited for: an allele is one of two or more versions of a DNA sequence; a person inherits two alleles, one from each parent.

title: Dominant Traits and Alleles (Talking Glossary of Genomic and Genetic Terms)
notes: Cited for: one copy of a dominant allele is enough to show the trait; the recessive allele's effect is masked.

title: Polygenic Trait (Talking Glossary of Genomic and Genetic Terms)
notes: Cited for: a polygenic trait, such as height or skin color, is influenced by two or more genes, and many are also shaped by the environment.

title: Is eye color determined by genetics?
publisher: MedlinePlus Genetics (US National Library of Medicine)
notes: Cited for: eye color was once thought to be one gene with brown dominant; OCA2, HERC2 and other genes set iris melanin in a continuum; blue-eyed parents can, uncommonly, have brown-eyed children.

title: Biology 2e, 11.1 The Process of Meiosis
notes: Cited for: 23 chromosome pairs give over eight million (2^23) genetically distinct gametes; crossing over swaps matching pieces, so two gametes are unlikely to match.

title: Is the probability of having twins determined by genetics?
publisher: MedlinePlus Genetics (US National Library of Medicine)
notes: Cited for: how identical (MZ) and fraternal (DZ) twins form; MZ twins in 3 to 4 per 1,000 births and DZ about twice as common; DZ twinning runs in families, MZ mostly does not.

title: Identical twin
notes: Cited for: the zygote splits into two cell masses; identical twins are genetically identical and always the same sex; fraternal twins share half their genes; twin studies of genes and environment.
